food.text: Archaeologist Professor Vasant Shinde says the earliest evidence for a dish similar to tandoori chicken comes from the Harappan civilization and dates back to 3000 BC. His team found ancient ovens at Harappan sites that resemble the tandoors used in Punjab today, and unearthed physical remains of chicken bones with char marks. Harappan houses had keyhole ovens with central pillars, used for roasting meats and baking breads.

Around 7000 BCE, agriculture spread from the Fertile Crescent to the Indus Valley, and wheat and barley began to be grown. Sesame and humped cattle were domesticated by the local farming communities. This began a cereal-growing tradition that shaped Indian cuisine.

Mehrgarh, in the Kacchi Plain of present-day Pakistan, is the earliest reliably dated Neolithic site in South Asia. Its early farmers used domesticated wheat and barley, kept sheep, goats and cattle, and lived in mud-brick houses.
By 3000 BCE, turmeric, cardamom, black pepper and mustard were being harvested in India. These are among the flavours that later became central to Indian cooking.

Around 7000 BCE, communities at Mehrgarh began investing more labor in preparing land and in selecting, planting, tending and harvesting particular grain-producing plants. They also domesticated sheep, goats, pigs and oxen, both humped zebu and unhumped types.
Castrating oxen turned them from mainly meat sources into domesticated draft animals. This shift at Mehrgarh made cattle useful for work as well as for food.

The aceramic Neolithic at Mehrgarh I in Baluchistan, dubbed the "Early Food Producing Era", lasted from about 7000 to 5500 BCE. The ceramic Neolithic that followed lasted up to 3300 BCE, blending into the Early Harappan period.

The Kashmir Valley holds multiple sites of the so-called Northern Neolithic, possibly dating as early as 3000 BC when the climate became warmer. Its slightly lower latitude made it a threshold where crops could be grown without special traits needed further north.

art.text: The rock shelters of Bhimbetka contain some of the world's oldest known cave paintings. The earliest Indian art is traced to prehistoric settlements of the 3rd millennium BCE.

The Bhimbetka rock shelters in central India hold the oldest known rock art in India and are one of the largest prehistoric complexes. The earliest paintings there are dated to 10,000 BCE, corresponding to the Indian Mesolithic.

The Bhimbetka paintings show animals, hunting and early evidence of dance from the Stone Age. Some scenes show hunters carrying bows, arrows, swords and shields. In one cave, a bison is shown in pursuit of a hunter while his two companions appear to stand helplessly nearby.

Bhimbetka is a UNESCO World Heritage Site made up of seven hills and over 750 rock shelters spread across 10 km. It lies in the Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh, about 45 kilometres south-east of Bhopal. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 2003.

The Bhimbetka rock shelters sit on the edge of the Deccan Plateau, where deep erosion has left huge sandstone outcrops. The many caves and grottos there contain primitive tools and decorative rock paintings. These reflect an ancient tradition of human interaction with the landscape that continues to this day.

Indian cliff painting evolved gradually over many thousands of years, with multiple locations holding prehistoric art. The early caves included overhanging rock decorated with rock-cut art, and natural caves were used during the Mesolithic period (6000 BCE). In some areas their use continued into historic times.
Painters at Bhimbetka used vegetable colours, and the paintings have endured through time. The drawings were generally made deep inside a niche or on inner walls, which protected them.

One Bhimbetka rock, popularly called "Zoo Rock", depicts elephants, barasingha (swamp deer), bison and deer. Paintings on another rock show a peacock, a snake, a deer and the sun. On a third rock, two elephants with tusks are painted.
The earliest examples of Indian art are petroglyphs such as those found at Bhimbetka, some of them dating to before 5500 BC. Production of such works continued for several millennia.

V. S. Wakankar classified the Bhimbetka drawings and paintings into seven different periods. He dated the earliest ones to the upper Palaeolithic, as early as 40,000 years ago. Some of the geometric figures there date to as recently as the medieval period.

Engravings on pottery and other artifacts show that the prehistoric people of Burzahom established contact with Central Asia and South West Asia. They also had links to the Gangetic plains and peninsular India.

war.text: The earliest rock paintings at the Bhimbetka rock shelters in central India are dated to 10,000 BCE. They show hunters with barbed spears, pointed sticks, and bows and arrows, and some scenes are interpreted as depicting tribal war between three tribes symbolised by their animal totems. In one cave a bison is shown in pursuit of a hunter while his two companions appear to stand helplessly nearby, and later paintings from the historic period mostly depict battles between rulers carrying swords, spears, bows and arrows.

Kot Diji, an ancient site on the Indus River opposite Mohenjo-daro, was occupied from around 3300 BCE. Its remains include a citadel built on high ground about 12 metres above the surrounding area, an early example of a fortified position in South Asia.

Excavations at Kot Diji, an early Indus Valley site on the Indus River, uncovered bronze arrowheads among its ancient artifacts, found alongside pottery, toy carts, and stone implements, though bronze at the site is otherwise noted as used mainly for personal ornaments.

science.text: From as early as 7000 BCE, communities at Mehrgarh, in the hills between the Bolan Pass and the Indus plain, put growing labor into preparing land. They selected, planted, tended and harvested particular grain-producing plants, and they also domesticated animals such as sheep, goats, pigs and oxen.

The South Asian Stone Age is divided into three broad phases based on tools and artifacts. The Mesolithic began around 10000 BCE after the Last Glacial Period, and the Neolithic began around 7000 BCE with the emergence of agriculture and settled life. The divisions have no precise chronological boundaries.

At Mehrgarh in the Kacchi Plain, early farmers used domesticated crops such as wheat and barley and kept sheep, goats and cattle. They lived in houses of mud-bricks. It is the earliest reliably-dated Neolithic site in South Asia.

The Soanian culture, named after the Soan Valley in Pakistan, made tools on quartzite pebbles and cobbles from river sources in the Siwalik Hills. Its assemblages generally include choppers, discoids, scrapers, cores and flake-type tools.

The Indus Valley Civilization built sophisticated water storage systems, including artificial reservoirs at Girnar dated to 3000 BCE. Such works belonged to a wider tradition of irrigation and water management in the region.

science.text: The earliest paintings at Bhimbetka are dated to 10,000 BCE, and they used vegetable colours. These pigments have endured through time because the drawings were generally made deep inside a niche or on inner walls.

Excavations at Bhirrana, along the ancient Ghaggar-Hakra River system in Haryana, gave a date of around 7600 BCE for its earliest levels. That dating has been questioned, because the cultural remains are of a more developed Chalcolithic stage using 4th millennium BCE ceramics.

culture.text: The rock shelters of Bhimbetka contain some of the world's oldest known cave paintings. They sit on the edge of the Deccan Plateau, where deep erosion has left huge sandstone outcrops full of caves and grottos.

Evidence for prehistoric religion in the Indian subcontinent comes from scattered Mesolithic rock paintings depicting dances and rituals. Neolithic agriculturalists in the Indus River Valley also buried their dead in ways suggesting spiritual practices, including notions of an afterlife and belief in magic.
The earliest religion followed by the peoples of the Indian subcontinent, including those of the Indus Valley and Ganges Valley, was likely local animism. It did not have missionaries.

Some of the earliest cave art was made in natural caves and under overhanging rock during the Mesolithic period, around 6000 BCE. Its use continued in some areas into historic times, and the tradition of cliff painting evolved over many thousands of years.

Stone Age sites such as the Bhimbetka rock shelters in central Madhya Pradesh and the Kupgal petroglyphs of eastern Karnataka contain rock art portraying religious rites. This art also holds evidence of possible ritualised music.

Punjabi culture grew out of settlements along five rivers, whose route served as an important link to the Near East as early as the Indus Valley Civilization, dating back to 3300 BCE. The name Punjab comes from the Persian words Panj, meaning five, and Âb, meaning water.

One of the Bhimbetka paintings shows a group of hunters running away from a rhinoceros, a vivid glimpse of the dangers these spear-armed hunters faced. It is one of many scenes at the site depicting the risks of prehistoric hunting.

The Bhimbetka caves and grottos contain primitive tools alongside decorative rock paintings. Together they reflect an ancient tradition of human interaction with the landscape, one that continues to this day.

Some scholars argue that during the mid-Holocene arid phase, Harappans shifted toward the sub-Himalayas in search of water. Trade in materials such as metal diminished, so they began making stone tools later recognized as Soanian, in a process viewed as deurbanization into smaller village-type settlements.
Some Bhimbetka paintings depict rats being driven out of their burrows so they could be caught, alongside fish and turtles caught in nets.
